LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Keep Trying, Learn, Celebrate & Be Yourself — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson builds the confidence shelf: four words that carry a child through the wobbles of learning anything — and one family ritual that makes sure the wins get their moment.

What is this?

Keep trying walks through the wobble, learn harvests every attempt, celebrate marks the wins (small ones loudest) and be yourself is the standing rule underneath: there is only one you, and that is the good news.

What does it mean?

Celebrate is the most skipped word in child-rearing — progress that is never marked quietly stops. A family that cheers small wins out loud raises children who attempt big things, because the trying has learned it leads somewhere good.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: wobbles are PART of trying, not a verdict on you; every attempt teaches something (the learn is automatic once you look for it); and being yourself is not the last step — it is the ground all four words stand on.

Why this matters

This card is the stamina of the class: feelings named, kindness chosen, skills drilled — and here is the fuel that keeps a child going when the zip sticks on the fortieth attempt. It also pre-loads the graduation: be yourself is what the whole path was for.

What it teaches

Persistence (the continue-through-difficulty muscle), learning orientation (attempt as data), celebration habits (marked progress sustains motivation), and self-acceptance — identity as the base camp for all achievement.

Words to learn

keep tryinglearncelebratebe yourselfwobblewinonly one you

Say this to your child

“"Here are the four words that make hard things possible. Keep trying — the wobble is part of it; every climber slips, every drawer sticks, every zip fights back on the first try. Learn — every attempt teaches something, even the ones that flop; especially those. Celebrate — when something lands, MARK it: cheer, dance, tell Dad, tell the neighbour’s cat; small wins counted loudly are what keep the trying coming. And be yourself — underneath everything, the standing rule: there is only one you in the whole world, and your way of doing things is allowed to be yours. Wobble, learn, celebrate — and stay you. That is the whole confidence recipe."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The confidence words."
  2. Read the panels: the fist-up girl KEEPs TRYING, the question-mark boy LEARNs, the sparkling boy CELEBRATEs, the thumbs-up winking girl BEs HERSELF.
  3. Tell the wobble story: something you failed at first, tried again, and what the second attempt taught — grown-up wobbles are the best teaching material in the house.
  4. Hold the celebration below — one HARD thing, cheered properly, effort named as the hero.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "wobble, learn, celebrate, repeat — and stay you the whole time."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the confidence: Keep Trying, a girl with a determined fist up; Learn, a wondering boy with a question mark over his head; Celebrate, a boy cheering under little sparkles; and Be Yourself, a winking girl with her thumb up — effort drawn as the hero, sparkle and all.

Ask your child

"What is a wobble — a stop sign or part of trying?" "What does a flopped attempt teach?" "Which wins do we celebrate — only the big ones?" "What is something ONLY you do?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Wobbles are part of it!" "I learned the wet sponge slips" (harvested) or the self-knowledge: "I do my dancing silly and that is MY way."

Out in the real world

Confidence moments stack daily: the shoe attempt (forty tries), the tower collapse, the first pedal stroke, the wobbly note at singing time. Mark each with the right word — "you kept trying," "what did that teach us," "CELEBRATE!" — and the words become the child’s inner soundtrack by default.

Try it together

The Hard-Thing Celebration: once a week, the family celebrates one HARD thing — confetti optional, cheering mandatory. The rule: the thing must have involved wobbles. Each person tells theirs (grown-ups first: the jammed printer counts), the effort is named as the hero ("you tried four ways!"), and the celebration is real: a dance, a dessert, a lap of the table. Effort that gets celebrated comes back for more.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are wobbles — part of it or a stop sign? Which wins get celebrated? What is the rule underneath all four?" Part of it, all of them (small ones loudest), be yourself — three answers and the confidence shelf is loaded.

Parent tips

Celebrate the specific, not the superlative — "you tried the zipper upside down AND the right way" beats "amazing!" every time; specificity proves you actually watched. And guard be-yourself from becoming a costume: the winking, thumbs-up child on the card is not a requirement — your quiet child’s be-yourself might look like standing at the edge of the party, watching, until ready. That counts. That is the word working.

This lesson pairs with the Keep Trying, Learn, Celebrate & Be Yourself flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).
